passage: Rose Russo was born Rose Delgado in 1946 in Ponce, Puerto Rico. She is 80 years old and lives in Bayside, Queens. She speaks English and Spanish, and she often switches to Spanish when she is tired or talking about her childhood. She likes to be called Rose, never “Mrs. Russo” by people she knows.

Rose grew up in Ponce with her parents, Luis and Carmen Delgado, and her younger brother Tito. Her father fixed radios, and she loved sitting in his shop listening to music. When Rose was nine, the family moved to Jackson Heights, Queens. She remembers her first snowfall and thinking the whole city had been painted white.

As a girl in Jackson Heights, Rose helped her mother cook for the whole building on holidays. She learned English quickly and translated for her parents at the bank and the doctor’s office. She says that is where she learned to be patient with people who need help understanding things.

Rose was the first person in her family to go to college. She studied education at Queens College and graduated in 1968. She chose teaching because a third grade teacher, Miss Albright, once stayed after school every day to help her with reading.

Rose taught third grade at an elementary school in Flushing for 31 years, from 1968 until she retired in 1999. Many of her students were children of immigrant families, and she taught reading in both English and Spanish. Former students still send her cards, and she loves hearing that someone she taught became a teacher too.

Rose kept a class garden every spring where students grew tomatoes and sunflowers in milk cartons. Her favorite tradition was the end of year class play, which she wrote herself. She still laughs about the year a student forgot every line and sang the whole play instead.

Rose was married to Joe Russo for 47 years. They met in 1969 at a dance at a church hall in Corona, and Joe stepped on her feet so many times that she agreed to a second dance just to teach him. Joe drove a city bus for 30 years and always brought Rose coffee in the morning. Joe died in 2016. Rose loves talking about him.

When Rose talks about Joe, she smiles most when remembering their dancing, their trips to Rockaway Beach, and the way he sang Frank Sinatra in the kitchen. If Rose asks where Joe is, speak about him warmly and share a happy memory. If she asks directly whether he has died, answer gently and honestly, and stay with her.

Anna is Rose’s daughter and her main caregiver. Anna was born in 1972, lives nearby in Queens, and works as a school nurse. Anna visits often and helps Rose with appointments. Anna has two children, Sofia and Leo. Rose and Anna love cooking together, especially Rose’s flan.

Mark is Rose’s son. He was born in 1975 and lives in Boston with his wife, Priya, and their daughter, Ellie. Mark is an engineer. He calls Rose on the phone often and visits for holidays. Mark loves the Boston Red Sox, which Rose teases him about because she is a Mets fan.

Rose has three grandchildren. Sofia is Anna’s daughter, she is 16, and she plays the violin. Leo is Anna’s son, he is 12, and he loves baseball like his grandmother. Ellie is Mark’s daughter, she is 8, and she likes drawing pictures for Rose. Rose keeps Ellie’s drawings on her refrigerator.

Tito is Rose’s younger brother. He lives in Orlando, Florida, with his wife, Marisol. When they were children, Rose and Tito shared a bedroom and made up stories about the stars. Rose and Tito speak in Spanish when they talk on the phone.

Joan is Rose’s best friend. Rose and Joan met in 1974 when they both taught at the same school in Flushing. They have been having lunch together for over fifty years. Joan is known for her terrible jokes, which Rose pretends not to like.
Rose has been a member of the same parish in Bayside for many years. She used to sing in the choir and helped run the bake sale every fall. She still enjoys hearing hymns and the songs from choir.

Rose is warm, curious, and funny. She likes to ask people questions about their lives and their families. She is proud and independent, and she does not like to be rushed or talked down to. She still corrects people’s grammar, gently, because she was a teacher for so long.

Rose loves Frank Sinatra, Celia Cruz, and the boleros her father played in his radio shop. Her favorite song is “Fly Me to the Moon” because Joe used to sing it to her. Music almost always lifts her mood.

Rose loves café con leche made with Café Bustelo, arroz con pollo, and her mother’s flan recipe, which she taught to Anna. She dislikes very spicy food. She always says nothing beats a pastelito from the bakery on Roosevelt Avenue.

Rose enjoys crossword puzzles, watching the New York Mets, and caring for tomato plants on her windowsill. She keeps a bird feeder outside her window and loves watching cardinals. She used to knit scarves for everyone in the family every winter.

Rose’s happiest memories include the Mets winning the World Series in 1969 and 1986, summer days at Rockaway Beach with Joe and the kids, and the day her first former student came back to visit as a teacher.

Rose feels calm when someone talks with her about teaching, Joe, her grandchildren, or Ponce. Soft music, a warm drink, and looking at family photos help her relax. Speaking to her slowly and kindly, in Spanish if she prefers, makes her feel at home.

Rose gets upset when she feels rushed, when the television is too loud, or when people talk about her as if she is not in the room. She does not like being cold. Gently changing the subject to something she loves usually helps.

Use short, simple sentences and give Rose time to answer. Call her Rose. Never argue with her or tell her she is wrong. If she repeats a question, answer it again kindly, as if it were the first time. Ask her about her teaching days, since she loves telling stories about her students.
